title: Greta Thunberg returns to COP after four years, calling the climate talks "hypocrisy" dominated by fossil fuel interests

 Thunberg Is Back at COP31: "These Negotiations Are Filled with Lobbyists"
 At the Antalya summit, Thunberg criticized industry lobbying while António Guterres called for windfall taxes on oil companies and binding fossil fuel transition plans.
 Mateo Moreno 
/
 Published Nov 12 2026, 2:15 PM EST Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 Swedish activist Greta Thunberg speaks to the media as she arrives at the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, on November 10, 2026. Global fossil fuel emissions are projected to fall slightly in 2026 due to the expansion of renewable energy and the oil price shock sparked by the Iran war, researchers said Tuesday. 
 Photo by Ozan KOSE / AFP via Getty Images 
 The Briefing 
 Greta Thunberg appeared at COP31 in Antalya for the first time since Glasgow 2021, denouncing the annual talks as captured by fossil fuel lobbyists who serve the industries profiting from inaction.
 Outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres used his final COP address to demand windfall taxes on oil companies, noting that nine major oil corporations are on track to earn more than $95 billion in just three months — over one billion dollars a day.
 With the United States absent for a second consecutive year and the leaders of France, Germany, and Italy skipping the Leaders' Summit, the November 9–20 negotiations open under a cloud of diminished diplomatic weight and low expectations for binding progress.
 A Familiar Voice Returns — Sharper Than Ever 
 Five years after dismissing world leaders' pledges in Glasgow as "blah, blah, blah," Greta Thunberg walked back into a United Nations climate conference on Tuesday — her first appearance at a COP since 2021. The 23-year-old Swedish activist arrived at the Antalya Expo Center as thousands of youth delegates from across the globe gathered in Turkey's Mediterranean resort city for talks running through November 20. 
 Her reappearance was more than symbolic. Since Glasgow, Thunberg had largely stepped away from the COP circuit, redirecting her public engagement toward Palestinian rights and anti-war activism. Her decision to return to Antalya was widely read as a deliberate statement: the structural problems she once encapsulated in a single phrase remain intact, and a newer generation of climate advocates needed a unifying presence at the table. 
 The Lobbyist Charge: Industry Infiltration in the Negotiating Halls 
 Speaking to reporters as she arrived, Thunberg was direct. She called the annual talks "a hypocrisy," accusing host governments of using COP as a platform to "whitewash themselves" rather than enact meaningful change. The negotiations, she said, are filled with lobbyists "paid by the very destructive industries" that profit from continued fossil fuel dependence — and the political and economic systems sustaining this arrangement have become "incompatible with human nature." 
 That accusation carries documented weight. At last year's COP30 in Belém, Brazil, the Kick Big Polluters Out coalition recorded 1,602 fossil fuel industry representatives with accreditation to the summit — roughly one for every 25 participants, the highest ratio ever measured at a UN climate conference. Sector representatives from oil, gas, and coal were often embedded within official national delegations, frequently operating without the transparency requirements that might have constrained their reach inside sensitive negotiating spaces. 
 Thunberg argued that whatever technical progress occurs inside the halls is secondary as long as the fundamental logic of the process remains unchanged. The goal, she maintained, should be protecting people and the planet — not shielding the interests of "a lucky few" at the expense of the " global majority ." 
 Guterres Marks His Final COP With a Blunt Warning 
 The tone inside the halls was set partly by outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres, attending COP31 as his final climate conference before leaving office at year's end. Addressing world leaders in Antalya, Guterres called the moment a "moment of truth" and trained his sharpest language on the fossil fuel industry's windfall earnings amid the global energy crisis triggered by the Iran conflict. 
 Calling on governments to impose taxes on those exceptional profits, Guterres pointed out that nine major oil companies are on track to earn more than $95 billion in just three months. "That is more than one billion dollars a day," he told delegates. He urged all nations to submit national roadmaps for ending their production and consumption of coal, oil, and gas with "clear timelines," and demanded that governments treat the transition away from fossil fuels as an economic and security imperative — not merely a climate one. 
 Low Expectations in a Diplomatically Diminished Room 
 The choice of hosts has drawn its own scrutiny. Turkey holds the COP31 presidency while Australia serves as President of Negotiations in an unusual shared-leadership structure agreed at COP30 in Belém. Yet both countries still rely on fossil fuels for 60% and 56% of their electricity generation respectively, according to Climate Change News, and each has approved new extraction projects this year. Turkey drew additional criticism during the summit's opening week after announcing new domestic oil field discoveries — a development that activists characterized as fundamentally at odds with the spirit of the talks. 
 Few analysts anticipate binding breakthroughs from the Antalya negotiations. Nations continue to navigate an energy price shock linked to the Iran war and ongoing conflict in Ukraine, reducing the political appetite for rapid transitions. The momentum from the 2023 COP28 agreement in Dubai — the first to call explicitly for a move away from fossil fuels — dissipated across two successive COPs without producing a binding roadmap. Brazil's voluntary fossil fuel transition framework, formally presented at COP31, now faces uncertain uptake from individual governments. Turkey's signature electrification pledge — raising electricity's share of global consumption from roughly 23% today to 35% by 2035 — has drawn criticism for not specifying that the additional power must come from clean energy sources. 
 At the diplomatic level, absences speak loudly. The United States — the planet's second-largest carbon polluter — has skipped COP for the second consecutive year under President Donald Trump's climate rollback agenda. The leaders of France, Germany, and Italy are also absent from the two-day Leaders' Summit in Antalya, a gap that smaller and climate-vulnerable nations have condemned as a failure to convert high-minded rhetoric into actual commitment. 
 Youth Voices Rally as the Clock Keeps Running 
 Even as the diplomatic halls registered those absences, the activist areas of the summit energized at Thunberg's arrival. Amber Turner, a fellow with the Alliance of Small Island States, said she hoped the activist's presence would "remind us why we started this work" — to drive meaningful change, hold decision-makers accountable, and build a better future for all. Kamori Osthananda, a youth negotiator within Thailand's official delegation, called Thunberg's appearance "symbolic" and expressed hope it would pressure the COP toward "real action and implementation." Singaporean environmentalist Qiyun Woo said Thunberg "adds to the demands of a generation" that must live with the full consequences of whatever deals — or failures — emerge from Antalya. 
 Thunberg balanced the tension between desperate hope and unflinching clarity. She acknowledged the need to "hold on to every positive sign we can get" in a moment this critical — while insisting that incremental wins cannot substitute for the structural transformation the moment demands. The process, she maintained, must ultimately exist to protect people and the planet, not to insulate a narrow elite from accountability. 
 " Climate change is threatening everything," she said. "Everything and everyone we love is at stake." 
 Negotiations in Antalya continue through November 20.
